entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0600: Vulnerability in kube-client
entry.summary: `openssl-tls` trusts OpenSSL's default CA store in addition to the configured cluster CA
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0600

openssl-tls trusts OpenSSL's default CA store in addition to the configured cluster CA
Reported
November 24, 2026
Issued
November 25, 2026
Package
kube-client (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability
Categories
  • crypto-failure
Keywords
#tls #openssl #certificate #kubernetes
Aliases
  • GHSA-hm5x-4x3m-4w8m
References
  • https://github.com/kube-rs/kube/commit/bc27fdc58380d8ba78347145999193e00fe1b030
  • https://github.com/kube-rs/kube/pull/2170
CVSS Score
6.8 MEDIUM
CVSS Details
Attack Vector
Adjacent
Attack Complexity
High
Privileges Required
None
User Interaction
None
Scope
Unchanged
Confidentiality Impact
High
Integrity Impact
High
Availability Impact
None
CVSS Vector
CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N
Patched
  • >=4.2.1, <5.0.0
  • >=5.2.0
Unaffected
  • <0.64.0

Description

With the openssl-tls connector, configuring a cluster CA (certificate-authority, certificate-authority-data, or the in-cluster ca.crt) did not limit which server certificates were trusted. The connector started from OpenSSL's default verify paths and added the configured roots to that store, so a server certificate chaining to any root in OpenSSL's default store passed trust validation. The certificate still had to be valid for the server name the client connects to. client-go and the rustls-tls connector trust only the configured CA.

An attacker on the path between the client and the apiserver who presents such a certificate, for example from a TLS inspection proxy whose root is installed on the machine, could complete the handshake and receive the client's requests, including bearer tokens.

This advisory covers the openssl-tls connector, added in 0.64.0, when a cluster CA is configured. The connector is used by Client::try_default(), Client::try_from(Config) and ClientBuilder::try_from(Config) whenever they select OpenSSL, by the ConfigExt::openssl_https_connector, openssl_https_connector_with_connector and openssl_ssl_connector_builder methods even when rustls-tls is also enabled, and since 4.2.0 for TLS to an https:// proxy.

Which connector the constructors select depends on the version. Since 0.86.0, rustls-tls is the default and takes precedence when both features are enabled. From 0.71.0 to 0.85.x, openssl-tls was a default feature of kube (and of kube-client up to 0.82.2) and took precedence over rustls-tls. The kube crate re-exports kube-client, so the same kube versions are affected.

The flaw was corrected in 5.2.0 and 4.2.1 by installing a certificate store that holds only the configured root certificates. After upgrading, an https:// proxy or a CA bundle that relied on OpenSSL's default store may need its CA added to the kubeconfig CA bundle. On older versions, switching the client to the rustls-tls connector avoids the issue.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0597: Unsoundness in hugepage-rs
entry.summary: `hugepage_rs::Box::new` may cause undefined behavior when initializing memory
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0597

hugepage_rs::Box::new may cause undefined behavior when initializing memory
Reported
October 28, 2026
Issued
November 24, 2026
Package
hugepage-rs (crates.io)
Type
INFO Unsound
References
  • https://github.com/cppcoffee/hugepage-rs/issues/9
  • https://github.com/cppcoffee/hugepage-rs/pull/8
  • https://github.com/cppcoffee/hugepage-rs/releases/tag/v0.1.2
Patched
  • >=0.1.2
Affected Functions
Version
hugepage_rs::Box::new
  • <=0.1.1

Description

hugepage_rs::Box::new incorrectly initialized freshly allocated memory. Earlier implementations could either drop an uninitialized T or create a mutable reference before the memory contained a valid T, causing undefined behavior even when called from safe Rust code.

The issue was fixed in version 0.1.2 by using ptr::write(nn.as_ptr(), data) to initialize memory directly through a raw pointer.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0598: Unsoundness in hugepage-rs
entry.summary: `hugepage_rs::alloc` may cause undefined behavior with zero-sized layouts from safe code
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0598

hugepage_rs::alloc may cause undefined behavior with zero-sized layouts from safe code
Reported
October 27, 2026
Issued
November 24, 2026
Package
hugepage-rs (crates.io)
Type
INFO Unsound
References
  • https://github.com/cppcoffee/hugepage-rs/issues/7
  • https://github.com/cppcoffee/hugepage-rs/pull/8
  • https://github.com/cppcoffee/hugepage-rs/releases/tag/v0.1.2
Patched
  • >=0.1.2
Affected Functions
Version
hugepage_rs::alloc
  • <=0.1.1

Description

hugepage_rs::alloc was a publicly accessible safe function that forwarded a Layout to the hugepage allocator's GlobalAlloc::alloc implementation without enforcing its safety requirements. GlobalAlloc::alloc requires the layout size to be non-zero. However, the safe wrapper allowed callers to pass a zero-sized Layout, violating this precondition without using unsafe. Affected versions therefore exposed an unsafe allocation precondition through safe Rust code, violating Rust's soundness guarantees.

The upstream repository fixed this in version 0.1.2 by marking alloc as unsafe and documenting its non-zero-layout requirement.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0599: Vulnerability in xmloxide
entry.summary: Stack overflow from unbounded recursion in DTD content-model parsing
entry.content:

RUSTSEC-2026-0599

Stack overflow from unbounded recursion in DTD content-model parsing
Reported
July 20, 2026

CVSS Score
7.5 HIGH
CVSS Details
Attack Vector
Network
Attack Complexity
Low
Privileges Required
None
User Interaction
None
Scope
Unchanged
Confidentiality Impact
None
Integrity Impact
None
Availability Impact
High
CVSS Vector
CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H
Patched
  • >=0.4.4

Description

xmloxide's DTD parser recursed without a depth bound when parsing the parenthesised content model of an <!ELEMENT> declaration. A small document whose internal DTD subset contains many nested ( drives unbounded mutual recursion between DtdParser::parse_content_particle and DtdParser::parse_content_spec_group, exhausting the stack and aborting the process.

The internal DTD subset is parsed during ordinary document parsing, so this is reachable through the default parse entry points (for example Document::parse_str) on any input that carries a DOCTYPE. The existing ParseOptions::max_depth limit does not prevent it: it bounds element nesting, not DTD content-model nesting. A stack overflow cannot be caught as an error, so any process that parses attacker-controlled XML with xmloxide can be crashed with a small payload.

Fixed in 0.4.4: a parenthesis-nesting depth counter is threaded through the content-model parser, and nesting deeper than 256 levels is rejected with a normal ParseError. Well-formed DTDs are unaffected.

Applications that cannot upgrade should reject or strip the DOCTYPE from untrusted input before parsing.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0596: Vulnerability in etherparse
entry.summary: Out-of-bounds read when iterating over IPv6 extension headers of laxly parsed packets
entry.content:

RUSTSEC-2026-0596

Out-of-bounds read when iterating over IPv6 extension headers of laxly parsed packets
Reported

etherparse (crates.io)

CVSS Score

CVSS Details
Attack Vector

Privileges Required

Unchanged
Confidentiality Impact
Low

Availability Impact
High
CVSS Vector
CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:H
Patched
  • ^0.14.4
  • ^0.15.1
  • ^0.16.1
  • ^0.17.1
  • ^0.18.3
  • ^0.19.1
  • ^0.20.4
  • >=0.21.1
Unaffected
  • <0.14.0

Description

Iterating over malformed or truncated IPv6 extension headers can cause out-of-bounds reads when the packet was parsed using one of the lax parsing functions (e.g. via Ipv6ExtensionsSlice::from_slice_lax or LaxSlicedPacket).

Lax parsing stops at the first invalid or truncated extension header and returns the headers parsed up to that point. The "next header" field of the last returned header can then refer to a header that is not part of the slice. Ipv6ExtensionSliceIter followed it without checking the remaining length.

A crafted or truncated IPv6 packet can cause a crash or expose memory located behind the packet to the application. Users who do not iterate over the IPv6 extension headers of laxly parsed packets are not affected.

As a workaround, do not iterate over the IPv6 extension headers if lax parsing reported an error.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

Description

When writing an encrypted parquet file with a column with bloom filters, the header and bitsets of the bloom filter are written in plaintext in the final parquet.

Patched versions now reject writing bloom filters when encryption is enabled, raising an error at runtime.

Existing encrypted parquet files written with bloom filters are still vulnerable, and it is recommended to rewrite those files with bloom filters disabled if possible.

Credit to Yanzhi Xin (autoCAT6) for finding this.

entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0594: Vulnerability in cookie
entry.summary: Private cookie nonces can repeat in processes that fork
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0594

Private cookie nonces can repeat in processes that fork
Reported
November 23, 2026
Issued
November 23, 2026

cookie (crates.io)

CVSS Score
6.5 MEDIUM
CVSS Details
Attack Vector
Network

Scope

Confidentiality Impact
Low
Integrity Impact

Availability Impact
None
CVSS Vector
CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N
Patched
  • >=0.18.3
Unaffected
  • <0.11.3
  • >=0.12.0, <0.14.0
Affected OSes
  • linux
  • macos
  • freebsd
  • netbsd
  • openbsd
  • dragonfly
  • solaris
  • illumos
  • android
  • ios
Affected Functions
Version
cookie::PrivateJar::add
  • >=0.11.3, <0.12.0
  • >=0.14.0, <0.18.3
cookie::PrivateJar::add_original
  • >=0.11.3, <0.12.0
  • >=0.14.0, <0.18.3

Description

Who is affected

Only applications that call fork() and then add private (encrypted) cookies on the thread that forked, in more than one of the resulting processes. This is an uncommon way to deploy a Rust web application. In particular:

  • Rocket is not affected.
  • axum is not affected as normally run. It is affected only when an application forks worker processes itself and runs each on a current-thread runtime. See "Rocket and axum" below.
  • Applications that never fork are not affected. This includes all applications on Windows.
  • Signed cookies (SignedJar) are not affected.

The exact conditions are listed under "Conditions" below.

Description

Private cookies are sealed with AES-256-GCM using a random 96-bit nonce. Affected versions drew the nonce from rand's thread-local generator, rand::thread_rng(). That generator hands out bytes from an internal buffer and only notices that the process has forked when the buffer is refilled. A process that forks therefore continues, in both the parent and the child, from the same buffered bytes, and the private cookies sealed first on each side of the fork use the same nonces.

Impact

Reusing a nonce under the same key breaks AES-GCM. From two private cookies that share a nonce, an attacker can:

  • recover the XOR of the two plaintexts, and thus either plaintext if the other is known, and
  • recover the GHASH authentication key and forge private cookies, with a name and value of their choosing, that the application accepts as authentic.

The nonce is the first 12 bytes of a private cookie's (base64-decoded) value, so a repeated nonce is visible to anyone who holds two such cookies.

Exploitation requires the uncommon deployment described above, and only the first private cookies added after a fork are affected: at most 21 per process. An attacker must obtain two of them, from two different processes.

Conditions

All of the following must hold:

  1. The target is a Unix-like system and the process calls fork() without a subsequent exec().
  2. The thread that calls fork() used rand::thread_rng() at any point before the fork. Any use counts, including Key::generate(), adding a private cookie, or a call made by an unrelated crate.
  3. After the fork, private cookies are added on that same thread in two or more of the resulting processes: the parent and a child, or several children.
  4. Those processes use the same Key.

When they hold, at most the first 21 private cookies added on that thread in each process share nonces. After that the generator reseeds and the processes diverge.

The following are not affected:

  • Applications that never fork, including all applications on Windows.
  • Processes in which the forking thread did not use rand::thread_rng() before the fork.
  • Private cookies added on threads that were created after the fork. This includes servers that fork and then start a multi-threaded async runtime in each child.
  • Signed cookies (SignedJar), which do not use a nonce.
  • Versions 0.12.0 through 0.13.3, and 0.11.2 and earlier, which obtained nonces from the operating system via ring.

Rocket and axum

Rocket and axum were tested with cookie 0.18.2 by collecting the private cookies sent by each server process and comparing their nonces.

Rocket (0.5.4, CookieJar::add_private()) is not affected. Rocket does not fork, and it handles requests on worker threads of a runtime it creates when launched. No nonce was reused:

  • when launched normally, in a single process, or
  • when a parent process used a private cookie and then forked two worker processes that each launched Rocket.

axum (0.8.9, with PrivateCookieJar from axum-extra 0.12.6) is not affected as normally run. No nonce was reused:

  • when run in a single process on a multi-threaded runtime, or
  • when a parent process used a private cookie and then forked two worker processes that each started a multi-threaded runtime.

An axum application is affected only if it does all of the following:

  1. forks worker processes itself,
  2. runs each worker on a current-thread runtime on the thread that forked, so that requests are handled on that thread, and
  3. used rand::thread_rng() on that thread before forking.

In that configuration, the first private cookies sent by two workers reused nonces: 19 when the parent had added one private cookie before forking, and 15 when the parent had only called Key::generate(). No nonce was reused when the parent did neither.

Other frameworks and libraries that use this crate's PrivateJar were not tested. The conditions above apply to them as well.

Fix

Version 0.18.3 obtains nonces directly from the operating system's random number generator, which is not affected by fork.

Workarounds

If upgrading is not possible, any one of the following prevents the reuse:

  • Do not use rand::thread_rng(), directly or indirectly, on the forking thread before forking. In particular, create the Key with Key::from() or Key::derive_from() rather than Key::generate() before the fork.
  • In each child, immediately after forking, read and discard at least 256 bytes from rand::thread_rng() before adding any private cookie.
  • Add private cookies only on threads created after the fork.

Applications that ran in an affected configuration should rotate their Key.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

Validating Matrix Content URIs may panic

ruma_identifiers_validation::mxc_uri::validate
  • <0.13.0, >=0.2.3

Description

Using mxc_uri::validate may panic if the server name part of the URI is larger than 249 bytes. The affected versions assumed that the length of the first part of the URI (mxc://{server_name}) would fit into a NonZeroU8, but the length of the server name wasn't validated and the Matrix specification actually allows the server name to have a maximum length of 261 bytes.

entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0593: Vulnerability in pqcrypto-dilithium
entry.summary: Dilithium verification accepts non-conforming signatures with the `avx2` feature
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0593

Dilithium verification accepts non-conforming signatures with the avx2 feature
Reported
November 21, 2026
Issued
November 22, 2026
Package
pqcrypto-dilithium (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability
Categories
  • crypto-failure
Keywords
#dilithium #signature #verification #avx2
References
  • https://github.com/RatioLabsEU/pqc-field-notes/tree/main/advisories/2026-mldsa-avx2-verifier
  • https://github.com/pq-crystals/dilithium/issues/113
  • https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0586.html
Patched
no patched versions
Affected Architectures
  • x86_64

Description

With the default avx2 feature on x86_64 and a CPU that supports AVX2, pqcrypto-dilithium verifies signatures with PQClean's AVX2 implementation of Dilithium. That implementation predates two upstream fixes (pq-crystals/dilithium#113, 3 June 2026), the same ones described in RUSTSEC-2026-0586 for pqcrypto-mldsa:

  • the verifier does not check that the infinity norm of z is below γ1 − β, so it accepts signatures that the crate's own portable implementation rejects;
  • use_hint_avx() mishandles a boundary case, so one class of valid signatures is rejected.

Creating an accepted out-of-bound signature requires the private key. The practical effect is that verification results differ between this crate with AVX2 and the same crate without it.

Tested on version 0.5.0: for each of dilithium2, dilithium3 and dilithium5, 20 signatures with z out of bound are accepted with AVX2 and rejected by the portable code, and 2 valid signatures that exercise the use_hint boundary are rejected with AVX2 and accepted by the portable code. This crate implements a pre-standard version of the scheme, so the Wycheproof ML-DSA vectors do not apply; the test signatures are built with the crate's own signer.

The crate is unmaintained (see RUSTSEC-2024-0380) and no patched version is expected. Disabling the avx2 feature avoids the affected code.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0590: Vulnerability in secure-gate
entry.summary: `Fixed` and `Dynamic` secret wrappers were not zeroized on drop
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0590

Fixed and Dynamic secret wrappers were not zeroized on drop
Reported
March 17, 2026
Issued
November 22, 2026
Package
secure-gate (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability
Categories
  • memory-exposure
Keywords
#zeroize #drop #secrets
References
  • https://github.com/Slurp9187/secure-gate/blob/main/SECURITY.md#past-advisory
Patched
  • >=0.8.0-rc.1
Unaffected
  • <0.5.0

Description

In affected versions, the Fixed<T> and Dynamic<T> wrappers (and the FixedNoClone / DynamicNoClone variants in 0.6.x) did not wipe their contents when dropped. The types implemented the zeroize::ZeroizeOnDrop marker trait, which has no methods and does nothing by itself, but had no Drop implementation. The documentation stated that secrets were zeroized on drop.

A secret held in one of these wrappers stayed in the freed stack or heap memory after the wrapper went out of scope, where it could be read by anything able to observe that memory later, such as a core dump, swap, or a separate memory disclosure bug.

Versions before 0.5.0 are not affected: with the default zeroize feature they stored the secret in secrecy::SecretBox or zeroize::Zeroizing, both of which wipe on drop.

The flaw was fixed by making zeroize a required dependency, bounding the wrappers on T: Zeroize, and adding Drop implementations that call zeroize(). The first published release with the fix is 0.8.0-rc.1; the first stable release is 0.8.0. All affected versions have been yanked from crates.io.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0591: Security notice about secmem-proc
entry.summary: Ineffective default DACL on Windows
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0591

Ineffective default DACL on Windows
Reported
October 27, 2026
Issued
November 22, 2026
Package
secmem-proc (crates.io)
Type
INFO Notice
Categories
  • memory-exposure
References
  • https://github.com/niluxv/secmem-proc/issues/13
Patched
  • >=0.3.9
Affected OSes
  • windows

Description

On Windows, affected versions of this crate do not provide the intended security-enhancement. In particular, any process running under the same user as the hardened process can reset our DACL, and thus bypass the protection the DACL should have provided. Usage of the crate however does not actively harm security.

On affected version, an explicit owner SID (taken from the process token) was used for the DACL. However, Windows implicitly grants extra access rights to the well-known "owner rights" SID, unless it occurs in the DACL, which it did not. This allows any process under the same user to reset the DACL of our process, making this defence effectively useless. The new code uses the well-known "owner rights" SID, preventing the attack.

The default hardening setup is fixed in version 0.3.9. Users creating a custom DACL with the API from the win_acl module need to manually update their code to get the security enhancement. They are strongly advised to use a well-known "owner rights" SID created using the new win_acl::SidRef::well_known (introduced in version 0.3.9) in their DACL instead of the owner SID returned by win_acl::TokenUser::sid.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0592: Vulnerability in url
entry.summary: Stack overflow in `Url::origin()` on nested `blob:` URLs
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0592

Stack overflow in Url::origin() on nested blob: URLs
Reported
November 20, 2026
Issued
November 22, 2026
Package
url (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability
Categories
  • denial-of-service
Keywords
#stack-overflow #recursion #blob
Aliases
  • GHSA-hrj5-67jp-wqp9
References
  • https://github.com/servo/rust-url/pull/1186
Patched
  • >=2.5.9
Affected Functions
Version
url::Url::origin
  • <=2.5.8
url::quirks::origin
  • <=2.5.8

Description

In url 2.5.8 and earlier, Url::origin() handled a blob: URL by parsing its path as another URL and calling itself on the result. It did so regardless of the inner URL's scheme, blob included. Each blob: prefix cost one stack frame, with no limit on nesting depth. Url::parse() accepts a URL with 10,000 blob: prefixes followed by https://example.com/ (50,020 bytes in total); calling Url::origin() on it overflowed the default 2 MiB stack of a spawned thread.

A stack overflow aborts the whole process, and catch_unwind() does not catch it. One such URL crashes any program that calls Url::origin() on untrusted input. url::quirks::origin() also calls Url::origin(). For example, Servo's URL.origin DOM getter calls url::quirks::origin(), so a script on a page can trigger the overflow.

url 2.5.9 follows the URL Standard: Url::origin() takes the origin of the inner URL only when its scheme is http, https, or file, returns an opaque origin otherwise, and never calls itself. A blob: URL with another inner scheme that previously produced a tuple origin, such as blob:ws://... or blob:blob:https://..., now returns an opaque origin.

Affected Functions
Version
tokio_rate_limit::tonic_middleware::IpKeyExtractor::extract
  • >=0.5.0, <0.11.1

Description

tonic_middleware::IpKeyExtractor is documented as rate limiting gRPC requests by client IP address, but on a standard tonic server it keys on client-supplied x-forwarded-for and x-real-ip headers. In 0.5.0–0.9.1, the extractor reads those headers directly; in 0.10.0–0.11.0, it first checks for a bare std::net::SocketAddr request extension—which tonic::transport::Server never supplies, as it provides TcpConnectInfo instead—and falls back to the same headers. Direct clients can therefore choose their rate-limit key to bypass per-IP rate limits and increase the number of tracked keys; without forwarding headers, 0.5.0–0.9.1 allow requests without limiting them and 0.10.0–0.11.0 reject them by default unless .fail_open() is enabled.

Applications are affected if they use GrpcRateLimitLayer with IpKeyExtractor (the tonic-support feature). The HTTP middleware's IpKeyExtractor reads ConnectInfo<SocketAddr> and is not affected.

Version 0.11.1 fixes IpKeyExtractor to honor a server-supplied SocketAddr override first and then read the TCP peer address from tonic's TcpConnectInfo (which tonic::transport::Server attaches to plaintext connections and connections using its built-in TLS), without ever reading forwarding headers. Deployments behind a trusted proxy can use the new opt-in ForwardedIpKeyExtractor, which reads a single configured header (x-forwarded-for or x-real-ip) and is only correct when that proxy sets the header as documented.

If you cannot upgrade to 0.11.1, use a custom key extractor that reads the peer IP from tonic's connection information for the transport in use (including TLS) and rejects requests without a verified peer address before invoking the limiter, or restrict backend access to a trusted proxy that strips all incoming x-forwarded-for and x-real-ip fields and sets one x-forwarded-for value to the verified client IP on every request.

  • <0.10.4
sad_rsa::RsaPrivateKey::from_primes
  • <0.10.4
sad_rsa::RsaPrivateKey::validate

Description

RsaPrivateKey private-key construction, validation, and serialization can panic across three classes of inputs, as well as when re-encoding certain valid keys:

  • RsaPrivateKey::from_components and PKCS#1 or PKCS#8 private-key decoding (DER or PEM) can panic during validation when a supplied factor equals 1, because RsaPrivateKey::validate() let a factor of 1 reach a later check that panicked.
  • RsaPrivateKey::from_primes and RsaPrivateKey::from_p_q can panic during construction when a supplied factor is 0, 1, or even.
  • Prime recovery in RsaPrivateKey::from_components can panic when the private exponent is 0.
  • For a key, including a valid one, whose first prime occupies more limbs than the second, crt_coefficient, to_pkcs1_der, to_pkcs8_der, and serde serialization can panic.

An application that imports untrusted private keys or factors, or re-encodes such keys, can lose a worker, or the whole process when built with panic = "abort". Public-key parsing is not affected.

Fixed in 0.10.4, which rejects factors below 2, even factors, repeated factors, and a zero private exponent during prime recovery, and computes the CRT coefficient and re-encodes valid two-prime keys when the first prime occupies more limbs than the second.

If you cannot upgrade to 0.10.4, isolate the entire import, construction, CRT calculation, or serialization in a separate process and treat an abnormal exit as an operation failure, or use catch_unwind around the entire operation when panics unwind.

ML-KEM does not perform the FIPS 203 input checks

#ml-kem #fips203 #input-validation

Patched
no patched versions
Affected Functions
Version
pqcrypto_mlkem::mlkem1024::decapsulate
  • <=0.1.1
pqcrypto_mlkem::mlkem1024::encapsulate
  • <=0.1.1
pqcrypto_mlkem::mlkem512::decapsulate
  • <=0.1.1
pqcrypto_mlkem::mlkem512::encapsulate
  • <=0.1.1
pqcrypto_mlkem::mlkem768::decapsulate
  • <=0.1.1
pqcrypto_mlkem::mlkem768::encapsulate
  • <=0.1.1

Description

pqcrypto-mlkem wraps PQClean's ML-KEM implementation, which does not perform the input checks required by FIPS 203:

  • encapsulation does not perform the encapsulation key modulus check (section 7.2), so encapsulation keys with coefficients that are not reduced modulo q are accepted;
  • decapsulation does not perform the decapsulation key hash check (section 7.3), so a decapsulation key whose stored hash or embedded encapsulation key has been altered is accepted.

With the Wycheproof ML-KEM vectors, 108 / 112 / 116 invalid encapsulation keys (ML-KEM-512 / -768 / -1024) and 2 invalid decapsulation keys per parameter set are accepted.

This does not disclose key material. It is a FIPS 203 non-conformance, and an affected implementation can disagree with a conforming one about which keys are valid.

The crate is unmaintained (see RUSTSEC-2026-0161) and no patched version is expected. Migrating to a maintained implementation, such as the ml-kem crate, is recommended.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

entry.summary: ML-DSA verification accepts non-conforming signatures with the `avx2` feature

RUSTSEC-2026-0586

ML-DSA verification accepts non-conforming signatures with the avx2 feature
Reported
November 20, 2026
Issued
November 20, 2026

pqcrypto-mldsa (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability

  • crypto-failure

#ml-dsa #signature #verification #avx2
References
  • https://github.com/RatioLabsEU/pqc-field-notes/tree/main/advisories/2026-mldsa-avx2-verifier
  • https://github.com/pq-crystals/dilithium/issues/113
Patched
no patched versions
Affected Architectures
  • x86_64
Affected Functions
Version
pqcrypto_mldsa::mldsa44::verify_detached_signature
  • <=0.1.2
pqcrypto_mldsa::mldsa65::verify_detached_signature
  • <=0.1.2
pqcrypto_mldsa::mldsa87::verify_detached_signature
  • <=0.1.2

Description

With the default avx2 feature on x86_64 (non-Windows) and a CPU that supports AVX2, pqcrypto-mldsa verifies signatures with PQClean's AVX2 implementation of ML-DSA. That implementation predates two upstream fixes (pq-crystals/dilithium#113, 3 June 2026):

  • the verifier does not check that the infinity norm of z is below γ1 − β (FIPS 204, Algorithm 8, line 13), so it accepts signatures that conforming verifiers reject;
  • use_hint_avx() mishandles a boundary case, so one class of valid signatures is rejected.

Creating an accepted out-of-bound signature requires the private key. The practical effect is that verification results differ between this crate with AVX2 and conforming implementations, including this crate without AVX2.

The Wycheproof ML-DSA verification vectors reproduce both defects: with AVX2, 37 / 41 / 49 invalid vectors (ML-DSA-44 / -65 / -87) are accepted and one valid vector per parameter set is rejected.

The crate is unmaintained (see RUSTSEC-2026-0166) and no patched version is expected. Disabling the avx2 feature avoids the affected code. Migrating to a maintained implementation, such as the ml-dsa crate, is recommended.
